newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss bank says won't settle in Holocaust suit.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bank says won't settle in Holocaust suit.

text.p: Switzerland's biggest bank on Monday ruled out an out-of-court settlement of a $20 billion lawsuit filed in New York by a Holocaust survivor who says Swiss banks may be hiding her family's wealth.
Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) vowed to fight the class-action suit, which claims Swiss banks withheld accounts from the heirs of Jews murdered in the Holocaust.

The suit was filed last week in Brooklyn federal court by Gizella Weisshaus, 66, on behalf of all heirs of Holocaust victims who had deposited money and property in various Swiss banks for safe keeping as Nazi terror spread over Europe.
"This will not be settled out of court. There is no question of a settlement," UBS spokeswoman Gertrud Erismann told Reuters.
"We will fight any form of these accusations," she added.
The suit names UBS and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC), two of the country's three biggest banks and both major global players. It also accuses more than 100 unnamed banking institutions and individuals.
Swiss banks say they have already searched twice for such accounts since 1962 while UBS and SBC have both rejected the charges.
Erismann said it was unnecessary to use courts to pursue claims to accounts said to have belonged to Holocaust victims.

She noted that Swiss banks early this year opened a central ombudsman's office to help heirs search for such accounts. The office has received more than 2,300 inquiries and more than 700 detailed claims.

In addition, the Swiss Bankers Association in May agreed with world Jewish groups to set up an an international committee charged with checking bank records and ensuring banks were doing enough to locate and return lost Holocaust accounts.
"If Mrs Weisshaus has clues that her father deposited money in a Swiss bank, she should report the name of her father to the banking ombudsman," Erismann said.

Ombudsman Hanspeter Haeni's office circulates information from would-be heirs to the more than 300 Swiss-owned banks, who are required by industry guidelines to search their files for any matching accounts.
Haeni told Reuters the law barred him from commenting on whether Weisshaus had asked him for information.
